title: Doctor, Lawyer, Teacher
welcome_lead: Three classic settings reveal asymmetric talk in fine detail. Step into the surgery, the courtroom and the classroom.
meta_desc: Doctor-patient, courtroom and classroom discourse as case studies at A-Level English Language.
final_note: You have observed asymmetric institutional talk across three professions — same structural logic, different stakes.

concepts.def: Asymmetric talk featuring history-taking, diagnosis and treatment recommendations; doctors typically control topic.
Highly constrained — barristers ask, witnesses answer; closed and tag questions dominate cross-examination.
Sinclair & Coulthard's teacher Initiation, pupil Response, teacher Feedback structure.
Open questions invite narrative; closed and tag questions constrain — used by powerful participants to control.
Goffman's term — a speaker realigns within talk (e.g. doctor switches from clinician to confidant).
Tailoring talk to the specific audience — central to expert-lay communication.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Doctors typically open with an open elicitor (so what brings you in today?) then narrow into closed questions to confirm diagnosis hypotheses.

Research shows patients are often interrupted within 18 seconds — a measurable asymmetry.

Barristers exploit tag questions (You were at the bar that night, weren't you?) and closed yes/no questions to restrict witness narrative.

Witnesses lose narrative control; the lawyer authors the story.

Teachers ask known-answer questions — they already know the answer; the question tests the pupil. The third move (feedback) confirms institutional authority.

The IRF structure is so dominant that disruptive lessons often involve pupils refusing the response slot.
